research_text:
## Factual research brief

### 1. What `java.security.KeyPairGenerator` governs, and what the finding refers to

`java.security.KeyPairGenerator` is the JCA engine class for generating public/private key pairs for a selected algorithm. A generator is obtained through `getInstance(...)`, optionally initialized, and then used with `generateKeyPair()` or `genKeyPair()`. The algorithm argument to `getInstance(String algorithm)` is a standard algorithm name and provider selection determines whether an implementation is available. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

For the reported message:

> expecting one of RSA,EC,DSA,DiffieHellman,DH but found Ed25519

the relevant documented API value is the **algorithm string supplied to `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance(...)`**. In the cited CrySL rule, that first argument is bound as `algorithm`, and the rule’s first constraint allowlists only `RSA`, `EC`, `DSA`, `DiffieHellman`, and `DH`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

This is not an Oracle JCA statement that `Ed25519` is invalid or unsafe. Oracle’s Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification expressly lists `Ed25519` as a `KeyPairGenerator` algorithm for Ed25519 key pairs. Thus, the message identifies a mismatch with this rule pack’s allowlist, not an API-level rejection of the `Ed25519` name. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

### 2. Documented correct usage and official remediation guidance

**Documented usage**

1. Request a generator using a standard algorithm name via `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance(...)`. The one-argument overload uses the first registered provider supporting the algorithm; provider-specific overloads select a named or supplied provider. If no suitable provider supports the requested algorithm, the API documents `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))  
2. Initialize either:
   - with an integer key size, whose meaning is algorithm-specific; or
   - with an `AlgorithmParameterSpec`, optionally with an explicit `SecureRandom`.  
   Unsupported sizes produce `InvalidParameterException`; inappropriate parameter specifications produce `InvalidAlgorithmParameterException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
3. Generate a new pair with `generateKeyPair()` or `genKeyPair()`. The methods are functionally equivalent. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

**The API’s explicit recommendation:** explicitly initialize the generator instead of relying on provider defaults. Oracle states that a provider must supply and document a default when initialization is omitted, but defaults can differ across providers and can change in a future version. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

**What the official sources do not recommend:** The JCA documentation does **not** prescribe replacing `Ed25519` with RSA, EC, DSA, or DH as a response to an allowlist finding. It documents `Ed25519` as a standard `KeyPairGenerator` name. Whether the selected provider on a particular runtime supports it remains provider/runtime-specific. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

No initialization argument or runtime diagnostic was supplied here. Consequently, the API documentation supports no conclusion about a particular key-size error or parameter error.

### 3. Compatibility and documented migration information

**Persisted key material.** The JCA `Key` interface defines an external encoded form for use outside the JVM. `getEncoded()` returns the primary encoding when available; `getFormat()` identifies it. The documented common formats are X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` for public keys and PKCS#8 `PrivateKeyInfo` for private keys. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))

For Ed25519 specifically, RFC 8410 defines algorithm identifiers and ASN.1 encoding use for Ed25519 public and private keys in X.509/PKIX-related representations. That means the persisted or transmitted form identifies the key algorithm; it is not merely an interchangeable byte representation across asymmetric algorithms. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8410/?utm_source=openai))

**Wire formats and consumers.** JCA does not define one universal wire protocol for generated keys. The `Key` API describes an external encoding, while a protocol, certificate profile, keystore, peer, or signature consumer determines whether it accepts the relevant key algorithm and encoding. The supplied material does not identify any generated-key consumer, persisted format, certificate use, protocol, or peer capability; those compatibility facts remain unresolved.

**Platform support.**

- Java SE 15’s Standard Algorithm Names specification already lists `Ed25519` as a `KeyPairGenerator` algorithm, and Oracle documents EdDSA as implemented in Oracle JDK 15. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))
- This does **not** establish support in every runtime/provider configuration. The `KeyPairGenerator` API directs users to implementation release documentation for algorithms beyond the platform’s required set; the current required-algorithms list shown in the API does not list Ed25519. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
- Therefore, support on a target runtime must be established from that runtime’s Java version and installed provider set, rather than inferred from this finding.

**Migration path.** I found no JCA-documented automatic migration or conversion path from an Ed25519 key pair to RSA, EC, DSA, or DH key material. JCA documents reconstruction/translation through `KeyFactory` and compatible key specifications, but that is not documented as cross-algorithm conversion. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))

### 4. Exact CrySL rule matching and condition

**Requested rule source:**  
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl

The rule’s receiver type is explicitly:

```text
SPEC java.security.KeyPairGenerator
```

Its event-matching clause is, verbatim:

```text
EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(algorithm);
	g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: initialize(keysize);
	i2: initialize(keysize, _);
	i3: initialize(params);
	i4: initialize(params, _);
	Init := i1 | i2 | i3 | i4;

	k1: keyPair = generateKeyPair();
	k2: keyPair = genKeyPair();
	Gen := k1 | k2;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

Accordingly, the source names these matched methods:

- `getInstance` with either one argument—binding it as `algorithm`—or two arguments—binding the first and treating the second as `_`;
- `initialize` with either `keysize` or `params`, with an optional second `_` argument;
- zero-argument `generateKeyPair` and `genKeyPair`, binding their result as `keyPair`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

The rule **does constrain the parameter list syntactically**: it distinguishes one- and two-argument `getInstance` calls, one- and two-argument `initialize` calls, and zero-argument generation calls. Its declared object types are `String algorithm`, `AlgorithmParameterSpec params`, `int keysize`, and `KeyPair keyPair`; it does not spell out Java provider parameter types for the `_` placeholders. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

The order and relevant first condition are, verbatim:

```text
ORDER
	Get, Init, Gen
CONSTRAINTS
	algorithm in {"RSA", "EC", "DSA", "DiffieHellman", "DH"}; //BSI TR-02102-1 Recommends atleast 3000bits for keys
	algorithm in {"RSA"} => keysize in {4096, 3072};
	algorithm in {"DSA"} => keysize in {3072};
	algorithm in {"DiffieHellman", "DH"} => keysize in {3072};
	algorithm in {"EC"} => keysize in {256};
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

The rule also declares required prepared-parameter predicates for RSA, DSA, DH, and EC parameter-spec initialization, and ensures `generatedKeypair[keyPair, algorithm]` after compliant usage. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

**Can it match a method that merely shares the API method name?** No, not according to this rule text alone: its `SPEC` target is explicitly `java.security.KeyPairGenerator`. The rule does not declare a generic name-only match over arbitrary receiver types. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

### Source limits and unresolved points

- The raw GitHub URL is a moving `master`-branch source; the supplied rule hash does not identify a repository commit or CryptoAnalysis version. This research cannot establish that the scanned rule file was byte-for-byte identical to the rule version used by the detector.
- No code, resolved call target, provider, Java runtime version, initialization arguments, key encoding, persistence location, protocol, or generated-key consumer was supplied. Those facts are required to evaluate actual platform compatibility, but are outside what can be concluded from the documented API and rule text alone.
